claims.claim: Fiction is a prose narrative of imagined events: it is created from the imagination rather than being a factual presentation of events that are historically true.
The test for sorting a work between fiction and nonfiction is not whether its story can be proven true but whether the work claims to be true.
A story in which imaginary characters are set into real historical events is still classified as fiction.
Creative nonfiction (such as memoir and personal narrative) shares many traits with fiction, but its plots, settings, and characters come from real life rather than an author's imagination.

A roman à clef is a novel that portrays well-known real people more or less thinly disguised as fictional characters, and novels can fictionalize the author's own experiences; such works remain fiction because they do not claim to be factual report.
Fiction's principal elements include plot (the sequence of events that produces a coherent narrative), character, setting, point of view, theme, tone, and mood or atmosphere.
The narrator is the voice that relates the story, and narrators can speak in first, second, or third person; the narrator is a constructed voice distinct from the author.

Narrators can represent events in scene (narrating a sequence in enough detail, often through direct-speech dialogue, to create the illusion that it unfolds before the reader) or summary (compressing the duration of events), and dialogue is the spoken exchange between characters.

Genre labels such as literary fiction versus genre fiction (mystery, science fiction, romance, fantasy, crime) group works by convention and teaching practice; whether a work is called 'literature' is a matter of judgment, not a fixed fact, and the categories overlap.
A short story has a condensed plot that evolves over a short time span with few characters, while a novel is a substantial narrative with many characters, often spanning many settings.
Samuel Taylor Coleridge described the reader's 'willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith' in Biographia Literaria, chapter XIV.

Because fiction is invented, readers judge it by internal consistency with its own premises and by craft, rather than by correspondence to external fact; textual analysis treats fiction as a crafted object whose choices produce effects.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a work counts as fiction depends on factual accuracy or on the author's claim to truth.
positions: Some readers sort by verifiability: if the events check out, call the work nonfiction.
Standard literary treatments sort by the claim to truth: fiction does not claim its invented events happened, even when it is set in real history.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the claim-to-be-true test, which handles borderline cases: imaginary characters in real historical events remain fiction, while an unverifiable firsthand account is nonfiction if the author claims it really happened.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'literary fiction' versus 'genre fiction' is a value judgment.
positions: Genre labels can carry an implied hierarchy, with genre fiction treated as mere entertainment.
The distinction is a convention of publishing and teaching; the categories overlap and quality varies within both.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the labels as scoped classification tools, not quality verdicts, and says so explicitly.
